title: India Just Threw Open Its Bond Market to the World. For NRI Investors, the Timing Could Not Be Better.
excerpt: Tax exemptions, subsidised hedging, and a $3 billion corporate debt rush — India's most aggressive capital-market reforms in years are rewriting the playbook for overseas fixed-income investors, with Bloomberg index inclusion now weeks away from a decision.
body:
In the space of a single week, India has done more to open its bond market to foreign capital than it managed in the previous five years combined. The moves are sweeping, coordinated, and — for NRI investors who have watched Indian fixed income from the sidelines — potentially transformative.

The Reserve Bank of India and the Finance Ministry have rolled out a package that reads like a wish list foreign bond investors have been writing for years: complete tax exemption on government bond investments, subsidised hedging for foreign currency deposits, expanded access to long-dated securities, and incentives for banks and state-owned companies to raise capital overseas.

The market has responded instantly. Foreign investors bought more than $1 billion of Indian government bonds in just three trading sessions after the announcement — nearly matching the $1.6 billion purchased in the entire year to that point. Government bond yields have fallen 10 to 30 basis points across the curve, with shorter maturities seeing the sharpest declines.

"We believe that these changes are a game-changer for debt flows," said Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt at State Street Investment Management, which manages about $5.6 trillion in assets.

## The Corporate Rush

The ripple effects have been immediate. Indian companies, led by non-banking financial firms, are raising more than 310 billion rupees ($3.24 billion) through bonds this week alone — a pace that would have been unthinkable a month ago when corporate yields had risen to their highest levels in seven years.

The RBI's measures have pushed corporate borrowing costs down by 40 to 45 basis points virtually overnight. State-run REC raised three-year funds at a coupon of 7.34 per cent earlier this week, well below secondary market rates. NABARD secured the same rate after cancelling a similar issue in May when rates threatened to touch nearly 8 per cent.

The queue of issuers tells its own story: Bajaj Finance (85 billion rupees), Muthoot Finance (27.5 billion rupees), Bajaj Housing Finance (20 billion rupees), and L&T Finance (15 billion rupees) are all lined up. Tata Steel and Tata Projects are returning to the bond market after a 15-month absence.

State Bank of India and Bank of Baroda are preparing to become the first users of the RBI's subsidised hedging window for overseas borrowings, targeting about $500 million each in five-year dollar bonds. Merchant bankers expect $15 billion to $20 billion in inflows through this route over the next six months.

## The Bloomberg Gambit

Behind the immediate market moves lies a larger strategic play. Bloomberg Index Services deferred the inclusion of Indian bonds in its flagship Global Aggregate Index in January, citing "operational and market-infrastructure considerations." It promised an update by mid-2026.

That update is now imminent. Bloomberg is expected to seek investor feedback this month on whether Indian government bonds should join the index — and the timing of India's reform blitz is no coincidence.

India's finance minister met with RBI officials in the weeks before the tax cuts to push for entry into the Bloomberg index, according to a government official. The tax exemptions and expanded access directly address the concerns Bloomberg flagged in January.

If India is included, the implications are enormous. The Bloomberg Global Aggregate is tracked by trillions of dollars in assets. Inclusion would trigger automatic, durable inflows from passive funds worldwide — a structural shift in demand that would lower borrowing costs for years to come.

India has already been added to the JPMorgan Emerging Market Local Currency Index in June 2024, the Bloomberg Emerging Market LC Bond Index in January 2025, and the FTSE Russell Emerging Market Index in September 2025. The Global Aggregate would be the crowning entry.

## What NRIs Should Know

For diaspora investors, three specific changes deserve attention.

First, the RBI is now fully subsidising hedging costs on non-resident Indian foreign currency deposits with maturities of three to five years, raised before September 30. This means banks can convert NRI dollar deposits into rupees at no hedging cost, creating a cheaper funding source that is flowing into shorter-duration bonds and driving yields lower.

Second, the elimination of withholding and capital gains taxes on foreign investments in government bonds removes a friction that had long made Indian fixed income unattractive relative to other emerging markets. The yield on India's 10-year benchmark bond sits around 6.91 per cent — a meaningful premium over U.S. Treasuries, now delivered without the tax drag.

Third, all new 15-year, 30-year, and 40-year government bonds are now part of the Fully Accessible Route, which allows unfettered foreign access without investment limits. This opens the long end of the curve to NRI investors who want duration exposure to Indian rates.

## The Risks

None of this comes without context. India's reform push is born of necessity as much as ambition. The Iran war, now in its fourth month, has driven Brent crude above $94 per barrel. Foreign portfolio investors have sold a record $30.4 billion of Indian equities this year. The rupee has been under persistent pressure. Equity mutual fund inflows fell to their lowest level in a year in May.

The bond market reforms are, in part, a capital-account defence — an attempt to attract dollar inflows through the debt channel after equities have bled foreign capital. The risk is that the reforms work too well in the short term, attracting hot money that could reverse if global conditions shift.

"Investors are likely to wait for clearer visibility on the global backdrop before committing meaningfully," cautioned Krishna Bhimavarapu, APAC economist at State Street Investment Management.

But for NRI investors with a longer horizon, the structural changes — tax exemption, subsidised hedging, broadened access, potential Bloomberg inclusion — represent a genuine inflection point. Indian fixed income has been the forgotten asset class in most diaspora portfolios. That may be about to change.
